questions.q: A 4-week-old male infant presents with progressive, non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds. The infant remains hungry after vomiting. Exam shows mild dehydration and a small, firm epigastric mass. Labs show hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?
o: Sepsis; IV antibiotics and fluid resuscitation
Pyloric stenosis; correct electrolytes followed by surgical pyloromyotomy
questions.e: Classic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis ("olive"). Electrolytes and fluids must be corrected before pyloromyotomy.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with diarrhea and poor feeding. Serum sodium is 165 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate rehydration strategy?
o: Bolus followed by rapid hypotonic fluid
questions.e: Hypernatremic dehydration is corrected slowly (about 48 h, sodium drop no more than ~10-12 mEq/L/day) to avoid cerebral edema.

questions.q: A 14-month-old girl has nasal congestion, hoarse cough and fever for 2 days, then "noisy breathing". Drinking well. RR 38, T 38.4. Inspiratory stridor only when crying, resolves at rest. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Mild croup (no stridor at rest): single dose of oral dexamethasone. Racemic epinephrine is for moderate/severe croup with stridor at rest.

questions.q: A 4-day-old newborn has lost 5% of birth weight. The baby is breastfeeding well with adequate urine output. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
questions.e: Up to ~7-10% weight loss in the first week is physiological; birth weight is regained by 10-14 days.

questions.q: Marked leukocytosis with severe recurrent necrotizing bacterial infections in a child with a history of delayed separation of the umbilical cord most likely suggests:
questions.e: LAD: neutrophils cannot leave vessels, so high WBC, no pus, delayed cord separation (>30 days).

questions.q: An 11-month-old has 4 days of productive cough and congestion, now wheezing. Feeding slightly less but wet diapers normal. T 37.5, HR 130, RR 30, SpO2 95%, looks well, mild subcostal retractions and intermittent wheeze. Most appropriate next step?
o: Provide supportive care in the outpatient setting
Obtain nasopharyngeal swab for virologic testing
questions.e: Mild bronchiolitis: clinical diagnosis, no routine CXR or viral testing; supportive care at home if feeding and oxygenating well.

questions.q: A 6-year-old admitted for elective surgery is well-hydrated, afebrile, with normal glucose and sodium. Most appropriate maintenance IV fluid?
questions.e: Current guidance (AAP 2018) favors isotonic maintenance fluid with dextrose to prevent hospital-acquired hyponatremia (surgery = high ADH state).

questions.q: A 9-year-old boy has months of sneezing, nasal itching, clear rhinorrhea and congestion, worse in spring. Pale, boggy turbinates. Most appropriate approach?
o: Measure serum IgE only and prescribe oral decongestants
Allergy testing if needed and intranasal corticosteroids
questions.e: Allergic rhinitis: clinical diagnosis, intranasal steroids are first-line; allergy testing to identify triggers when needed.

questions.q: A 9-year-old took an unknown amount of aspirin 4 hours ago. Vomiting, tachypnea, tinnitus. T 38, RR 34. Salicylate 45 mg/dL, pH 7.48, HCO3 16, K 3.2, high anion gap. Next management step?
o: IV fluids only and repeat salicylate level in 6 hours
Activated charcoal and IV sodium bicarbonate infusion
questions.e: Symptomatic salicylate toxicity: decontaminate and alkalinize urine with bicarbonate (correct K). Dialysis is for very high levels (e.g., >90-100 mg/dL), AMS, renal failure, or pulmonary edema. Intubation can worsen acidosis.

questions.q: A 10-month-old has profuse watery diarrhea for 3 days, dehydrated and tachypneic. ABG: pH 7.18, PaCO2 30, HCO3 14. Most appropriate interpretation?
o: Metabolic acidosis due to bicarbonate loss
Metabolic alkalosis due to volume depletion
questions.e: Low pH + low HCO3 = metabolic acidosis (normal anion gap from stool HCO3 loss); low PaCO2 is respiratory compensation.

questions.q: A 6-year-old has 4 months of recurrent cough and wheeze triggered by football and colds. Mild end-expiratory wheeze, CXR normal. Which feature most supports asthma?
o: Productive cough with green sputum for 3 weeks
Cough and wheezing that improve with bronchodilator therapy
Fever and chills with chest pain
questions.e: Reversibility with bronchodilator is a key supportive feature of asthma.

questions.q: A 6-year-old has chronic constipation with painful defecation and stool withholding. Normal anus, fecal mass in the abdomen, occasional bright red blood on toilet paper. Diagnosis and initial management?
o: Functional constipation; stool softeners and behavioral modification
questions.e: Withholding + painful stools + fissure bleeding = functional constipation. Treat with disimpaction, osmotic laxatives (PEG), toilet training.

questions.q: An 8-year-old girl with seasonal allergic rhinitis has 6 months of episodic dry cough, dyspnea, chest tightness. Diffuse expiratory wheeze, FEV1 70%. Which drug is most effective at reducing bronchial inflammation?
questions.e: ICS are the main anti-inflammatory controller in asthma.

questions.q: A 6-year-old with eczema develops generalized urticaria, lip swelling, wheeze and hypotension shortly after eating peanuts. Initial management and key long-term precaution?
o: IM epinephrine; prescribe epinephrine auto-injector and emergency action plan
Nebulized salbutamol; reassure it is self-limited
Oral antihistamines; advise peanut avoidance only
questions.e: Anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg, anterolateral thigh) first. Discharge with auto-injector and action plan.

questions.q: A 25-day-old term infant has progressive jaundice, clay-colored stools and hepatomegaly. Total bilirubin 15, direct 9 mg/dL. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia + acholic stools = biliary atresia until proven otherwise; Kasai before ~60 days.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy wets the bed at night but is dry during the day. No urinary symptoms, normal exam. First step?
o: Reassure parents and start behavioral therapy (bedwetting alarm)
questions.e: Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis: reassurance, behavioral measures, enuresis alarm (desmopressin as alternative).

questions.q: A 9-year-old girl has fever, erythema, tenderness and edema over the left eye, with limited ocular movement and decreased visual acuity. Most appropriate management?
questions.e: Painful/limited eye movement and reduced vision = orbital (post-septal) cellulitis: IV antibiotics, urgent ophthalmology, CT orbits.

questions.q: A 2-year-old comes for routine developmental assessment. He is expected to be able to:
o: Ride a tricycle and tie shoes
Use 10 words and combine them into long sentences
questions.e: The solved PDF contradicts itself here: this 443 version highlights "ride a tricycle and tie shoes", but both 442 copies highlight "run and kick a ball". Run and kick is correct by standard milestones: tricycle is 3 y and tying shoes 5-6 y.

questions.q: A mother breastfeeds her child every 2-3 hours. Choose the appropriate answer:
o: It is appropriate to breastfeed on demand
The mother should wait for the child to cry
questions.e: On-demand feeding, 8-12 times/day in early infancy, is normal. Crying is a late hunger cue.

questions.q: A child with brucellosis treated with rifampicin still has fever after 10 days. Next step?
o: Continue rifampicin alone for one more week
questions.e: Brucellosis needs combination therapy (monotherapy relapses). In children <8 y: TMP-SMX + rifampicin; >8 y: doxycycline + rifampicin.

questions.q: A 5-month-old has had recurrent infections since 2 months including PCP pneumonia and oral thrush. Severe lymphopenia, absent thymic shadow. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Early opportunistic infections + lymphopenia + absent thymus = SCID (medical emergency; HSCT).

questions.q: A fetus is at high risk for Down syndrome and the mother wants a definitive invasive test to confirm trisomy 21. Most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: NIPT, NT and serum screening are screening tests. Diagnostic (invasive) karyotyping = CVS or amniocentesis.

questions.q: A 7-year-old unvaccinated child has fever and a vesicular rash in different stages of healing. Best management?
questions.e: Varicella. In a healthy child it is mostly supportive; oral acyclovir if started early / risk factors. IV is for immunocompromised or complicated cases. Among these options, oral acyclovir fits best.

questions.q: Which laboratory finding is most consistent with hemolytic anemia?
questions.e: Hemolysis: high retics, high indirect bilirubin, high LDH, low haptoglobin.

questions.q: A healthy 10-week-old has Hb 10 g/dL with normal MCV and no symptoms. Next step?
questions.e: Physiologic anemia of infancy (nadir ~8-12 weeks in term infants, Hb ~9-11), normocytic. No treatment.

questions.q: A neonate presents with respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Bowel in the chest (usually left, Bochdalek) = scaphoid abdomen + respiratory distress. Avoid bag-mask ventilation; intubate, NG decompression.

questions.q: A child has a hard thyroid nodule with cervical lymphadenopathy. Next step?
questions.e: Pediatric thyroid nodules carry higher malignancy risk; hard nodule + nodes needs US and FNA.

questions.q: A child started a new antiepileptic drug and 2-3 weeks later developed fever, rash, eosinophilia and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis?
questions.e: DRESS: latency 2-8 weeks, fever, rash, eosinophilia, organ involvement (liver). Aromatic AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine) are common causes.

questions.q: A neonate has metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia and mild hyperammonemia, with a family history of neonatal death. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Organic acidemias: high anion gap acidosis + ketosis +/- hypoglycemia, mild-moderate ammonia. Urea cycle defects give very high ammonia with respiratory alkalosis, no acidosis.

questions.q: A child has seizures lasting 3 minutes, only during fever. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Simple: generalized, <15 min, once in 24 h, age 6 m-5 y. Complex: focal, >15 min, or recurs within 24 h.

questions.q: A child has brief staring spells with eyelid fluttering and generalized spikes on EEG. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Childhood absence (4-10 y): many brief daily staring spells, 3 Hz spike-wave, provoked by hyperventilation. Treat with ethosuximide.

questions.q: A child can sit with support and shows interest in food. Most appropriate feeding recommendation?
questions.e: Signs of readiness around 6 months: start complementary foods, iron-rich first. No need to delay allergenic foods.

questions.q: A child's urine protein is negative in the morning and 2+ in the afternoon. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria: first-morning sample normal, protein appears after being upright. Benign.

questions.q: A 4-month-old infant has fever and gram-positive diplococci on culture. What is the organism?
questions.e: Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci = pneumococcus. Streptococci otherwise appear in chains.

questions.q: Schistocytes on peripheral smear after a diarrheal illness. What is the causative organism?
questions.e: HUS (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + AKI), classically after Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7.

questions.q: How do you screen a 25-week preterm for intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH)?
questions.e: Bedside cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle, recommended for infants <30-32 weeks.

questions.q: A full-term neonate has unilateral chest distension and respiratory distress. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Unilateral hyperexpansion with shifted heart sounds suggests pneumothorax. CDH typically causes a scaphoid abdomen; meconium aspiration is bilateral.

questions.q: A neonate with congenital CMV infection has jaundice. The intrahepatic cause of cholestasis is:
questions.e: Congenital infections (TORCH, including CMV) cause neonatal (giant-cell) hepatitis, an intrahepatic cholestasis. Biliary atresia is extrahepatic.

questions.q: At what age does a child ride a tricycle?
questions.e: Tricycle at 3 years (along with copying a circle, alternating feet up stairs).

questions.q: A 4-week-old well baby has a grade 3/6 ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge and a fixed, widely split S2. Most likely explanation?
o: Left-to-right shunt through the ventricular septum
Left-to-right shunt through the atrial septum
Right-to-left shunt through the ventricular septum
Right-to-left shunt through the atrial septum
questions.e: ASD: fixed wide split S2; the murmur is a flow murmur across the pulmonary valve (upper left sternal border), not from the defect itself.

questions.q: Reviewing growth charts, which one is abnormal?
o: 6-month-old girl with height on the 20th percentile
7-year-old boy whose weight dropped from the 90th to the 25th percentile over one year
questions.e: Crossing 2 or more major percentile lines is abnormal. A steady position on any percentile is normal.

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy has constitutional growth delay. Which statement is consistent with this diagnosis?
o: Prognosis for a normal adult height is good
He was undernourished during his first year of life
He was small for size at birth
Bone age is normal compared to chronological age
questions.e: CDGP: delayed bone age, late puberty, often family history of "late bloomers", normal final adult height.

questions.q: A 10-year-old develops facial swelling 8 days after treatment for tonsillitis. You suspect post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Which finding is most commonly associated?
questions.e: PSGN: low C3 that normalizes within 6-8 weeks. High ASO/anti-DNase B. Cola-colored urine, not clots.

questions.q: A 3-year-old comes for developmental assessment. He should be able to:
questions.e: 3 y: tricycle. Hop on one foot ~4 y, skip ~5 y, write name ~5-6 y.

questions.q: A 5-year-old has generalized edema and you suspect nephrotic syndrome. Which is mandatory for diagnosis?
questions.e: The solved PDF contradicts itself: the 443 copy highlights the proteinuria option, the two 442 copies highlight albumin <3 g/dL. Kept the majority answer. Diagnosis needs nephrotic-range proteinuria (>40 mg/m2/h) plus hypoalbuminemia; the 100 mg/m2/day threshold in option B is too low to be diagnostic.

questions.q: A febrile 3-month-old has a catheterized urine with 100,000 CFU/mL Klebsiella pneumoniae and >=5 WBC/HPF. Interpretation?
o: Normal finding in this age group
questions.e: Febrile infant + pyuria + >=50,000 CFU/mL of a single uropathogen from a catheter sample = UTI.

questions.q: A 4-month-old has tachypnea, tachycardia, hepatomegaly, a soft pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary markings, and normal saturations in all limbs. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Large VSD: heart failure at 1-3 months as PVR falls. Large defects give softer murmurs (less turbulence); small VSDs are loud and asymptomatic.

questions.q: What is the initial physical manifestation of puberty in males?
questions.e: Boys: testicular volume >=4 mL first. Girls: thelarche first. The growth spurt is late in boys.

questions.q: A 15-year-old girl has 2 months of fatigue, joint and muscle pain and a malar rash. Positive ANA, low complement, proteinuria. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Malar rash + arthritis + renal involvement + ANA + low complement = SLE.

questions.q: At a 4-month visit the grandmother says solids should have started at 2 months. What is the recommended age to introduce foods other than milk?
questions.e: WHO/AAP: exclusive breastfeeding to about 6 months, then complementary foods.

questions.q: An infant is born to an HIV-infected mother who had effective ART and undetectable viral load at delivery. The infant is on post-exposure prophylaxis. How is HIV status determined in the first months?
o: HIV DNA PCR at 2 weeks, 1-2 months, and 4-6 months
HIV RNA PCR at 6 weeks as the sole test
CD4 count at birth and monthly
questions.e: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta, so antibody tests are unreliable before 18 months. Use nucleic acid tests (DNA or RNA PCR) serially.

questions.q: A 2-year-old with days of vomiting and diarrhea is lethargic, tachypneic, with poor skin turgor, refusing oral fluids. Initial IV management?
o: Bolus of isotonic solution at 20 mL/kg
questions.e: Severe dehydration: 20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus, repeat as needed, then deficit + maintenance.

questions.q: A 6-month-old has 3 days of high fever, then a maculopapular rash appears as the fever subsides. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Roseola: high fever 3-5 days, rash appears when fever breaks. Can cause febrile seizures.

questions.q: A 3-year-old has fever, barky cough and stridor after 2 days of URTI. Vitally stable; inspiratory stridor only. Most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure that it is croup and send home
Go to the operating room to secure the airway
questions.e: All croup severities benefit from a single dose of dexamethasone (0.15-0.6 mg/kg).

questions.q: A 3-year-old has recurrent S. aureus skin abscesses, Aspergillus pneumonia, delayed cord separation (5 weeks), recurrent gingivitis, poor wound healing and marked neutrophilia. Most consistent immunodeficiency?
questions.e: Delayed cord separation + neutrophilia + gingivitis/periodontitis + poor wound healing = LAD.

questions.q: A 6-year-old girl has 8 months of intermittent left knee pain with morning stiffness, limping in the mornings, a warm effusion and flexion contracture. Which lab finding is most associated with increased risk of ocular complications?
questions.e: Oligoarticular JIA in young girls: ANA positivity carries the highest risk of silent anterior uveitis. Needs regular slit-lamp screening.

questions.q: A child drops to the floor crying, arching his back and screaming when denied a toy, twice a week, about 10 minutes each. Best advice?
questions.e: Temper tantrums are normal at 1-4 y. Planned ignoring (keeping the child safe) and praising good behavior.

questions.q: By which route is BCG vaccine given to a newborn?
questions.e: BCG is intradermal (usually left upper arm).

questions.q: A 2-month-old receives a combination vaccine (DTaP, IPV, Hib, HepB, PCV, rotavirus). Primary benefit of combined form?
o: Multiple antigens at once produce stronger immunity
More fever and local reaction to boost memory
questions.e: Combination vaccines improve compliance and timeliness by reducing injections.

questions.q: A 3-week-old has recurrent projectile non-bilious vomiting, irritability, weight loss and a firm olive-shaped epigastric mass. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Olive mass + projectile non-bilious vomiting at 2-8 weeks = pyloric stenosis. Confirm with ultrasound.

questions.q: A 13-year-old girl with constipation passes hard stools with streaks of bright red blood on the surface. No pain or systemic symptoms. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bright red blood streaking hard stool = anal fissure, the commonest cause of rectal bleeding in children.

questions.q: A 7-year-old with fever, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing: Na 138, Cl 96, HCO3 10, glucose 350. Which is the correct formula for the serum anion gap?
questions.e: AG = Na - (Cl + HCO3), normal ~8-12. Here 138 - 106 = 32, high AG (DKA).

questions.q: An 8-year-old becomes dizzy and short of breath during an exam, anxious and breathing fast. pH 7.55, pCO2 22, HCO3 22. Acid-base disorder?
questions.e: High pH, low pCO2, normal HCO3 = acute (uncompensated) respiratory alkalosis from anxiety hyperventilation.

questions.q: A 7-year-old often wakes terrified at night and clearly remembers a vivid dream the next day. Which is true?
o: The child does not remember the dream
questions.e: Nightmares: REM sleep, later in the night, child wakes fully and recalls the dream. Night terrors: NREM, early night, no recall.

questions.q: A 4-year-old is found collapsed, apneic, pulseless, with cold extremities. Best next step?
o: Rescue breaths only, since children arrest from respiratory failure
Two-finger compressions in the center of the chest to 2 cm
Compressions with one or two hands on the lower half of the sternum, ~5 cm (1/3 AP diameter), full recoil, 15:2 with two rescuers
Both hands on the upper sternum, 6-8 cm deep, 30:2 regardless of rescuers
questions.e: Pediatric CPR: 100-120/min, depth 1/3 AP (~5 cm child), full recoil, 15:2 with 2 rescuers (30:2 single rescuer).

questions.q: A 12-year-old has abdominal pain, vomiting, deep breathing, drowsy, tachycardic, hypotensive. Glucose 420, pH 7.12, HCO3 10, Na 130, K 4.2, urine ketones. Most appropriate initial step?
questions.e: DKA with shock: fluids first. Insulin starts about 1 hour after fluids are begun; never bolus insulin. Bicarbonate is not used routinely.

questions.q: A 6-year-old weighing 12 kg is in shock from severe dehydration. What volume of 0.9% saline should be the initial bolus?
questions.e: 20 mL/kg x 12 kg = 240 mL.

questions.q: A 12-year-old Saudi boy has fever, sweats, malaise and arthralgia after drinking unpasteurized camel milk on a farm. Most likely organism?
questions.e: B. melitensis (sheep, goats, camels) is the most common and virulent species in Saudi Arabia.

questions.q: A newborn has a sacral swelling covered by a thin membrane; myelomeningocele is suspected. Most appropriate next diagnostic step?
questions.e: MRI defines the defect, cord tethering and associated anomalies (Chiari II). Head ultrasound also screens for hydrocephalus.

questions.q: After vacuum delivery a newborn develops a progressive fluctuant scalp swelling that crosses sutures and extends to the orbits and nape of the neck. The infant becomes pale and tachycardic. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Subgaleal bleed: crosses sutures, extends from orbits to nape, can hold a large blood volume and cause shock. Cephalohematoma does not cross sutures; caput is not progressive.

questions.q: A 9-year-old with absence seizures on ethosuximide has been seizure-free for 2 years. Next best step?
o: Switch to valproic acid for maintenance
questions.e: After ~2 seizure-free years, AEDs are usually tapered gradually. Abrupt stopping risks rebound seizures. Childhood absence epilepsy usually remits.

questions.q: A 7-year-old with 3 days of gastroenteritis: vomiting stopped, diarrhea continues, well hydrated with normal exam. Father asks about diet. Advice?
o: Clear fluids only until symptoms resolve
Avoid milk and dairy until diarrhea stops
questions.e: Early refeeding with a normal diet shortens illness. No need for clear-fluid-only or routine lactose restriction.

questions.q: A 10-year-old on ICS with salbutamol reliever uses meds about 3 days/week, good technique and adherence, and had 2 viral exacerbations needing oral steroids this year. Next step?
o: Stop ICS and switch to LABA monotherapy
questions.e: Not well controlled on low-dose ICS despite good adherence: step up (ICS-LABA). LABA must never be used without ICS.

questions.q: A 3-day-old healthy, well-feeding term boy is jaundiced with predominantly unconjugated bilirubin. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Physiological jaundice appears after 24 h, peaks at day 3-5, unconjugated, in a well baby. Jaundice in the first 24 h is pathological.

questions.q: A 6-week-old has persistent jaundice with clay-colored stools and dark urine, otherwise well. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Prolonged jaundice (>2 weeks) with pale stools and dark urine = conjugated; biliary atresia must be excluded urgently.

questions.q: A 7-year-old has 6 days of fever to 40.2, tender cervical lymph nodes, maculopapular rash, BP 80/45, HR 140, Na 129, K 3.1, CRP 120. Most concerning long-term complication?
questions.e: Kawasaki disease (here with shock). Coronary aneurysms are the main long-term risk; IVIG within 10 days reduces it.

questions.q: A healthy 12-year-old girl has BP between the 90th and 95th percentile on routine visit. Next step?
o: Repeat BP on at least two additional occasions
questions.e: 90th-95th percentile = elevated BP. Diagnosis of hypertension requires repeated readings on separate visits.

questions.q: A baby girl can transfer objects between hands, sit with support and mimic sounds. What is her age?
questions.e: Transferring objects hand-to-hand appears around 6 months.

questions.q: A neonate has not passed meconium for 46 hours and has bilious (green) vomiting. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Failure to pass meconium in 48 h + bilious vomiting/distension suggests Hirschsprung. Duodenal atresia vomits in the first hours but usually passes meconium.

questions.q: A 2-year-old returns after her first febrile UTI, finished antibiotics yesterday, asymptomatic, normal exam. Next best step?
o: Reassurance and clinic follow-up in 2-6 weeks
Renal and bladder ultrasound (RBUS) after 2-6 weeks
Repeat urine culture to document sterility
questions.e: AAP recommends RBUS after the first febrile UTI in 2-24 month olds. Test-of-cure cultures are not needed. Timing varies by guideline; urgent US is for poor response or atypical UTI. Note: timing answer is Claude's reading, check your lecture.

questions.q: After C-section a baby had Apgar 1 and 3, needed PPV, intubation, compressions and IV epinephrine. What should be done to preserve neurological function?
questions.e: Moderate-severe HIE in infants >=36 weeks: cooling (33.5 C for 72 h) started within 6 hours.

questions.q: A full-term infant has acrocyanosis, no respiratory distress, SpO2 98%, pink mucous membranes. Next step?
questions.e: Acrocyanosis (blue hands and feet) is normal in the first days. Central cyanosis would need workup.

questions.q: A 9-month-old exclusively breastfed baby is not growing well. The mother says he feeds well; exam is normal and he is alert. Most likely reason for failure to thrive?
questions.e: Most FTT is from inadequate intake. At 9 months, exclusive breastfeeding without complementary foods is insufficient.

questions.q: A 5-year-old has chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating and FTT, family history of autoimmune disease, and positive tTG-IgA. Next step?
o: Upper GI endoscopy with duodenal biopsy
questions.e: Celiac disease: confirm with biopsy (or no-biopsy route if tTG >10x ULN with positive EMA per ESPGHAN) while still on gluten.

questions.q: A 6-year-old with FTT, irritability and confusion has glucose 50, ammonia 200 and elevated branched-chain amino acids in urine. A maternal aunt has a metabolic disorder. Primary mechanism?
o: Enzyme deficiency causing accumulation of toxic metabolites
questions.e: Inborn errors of metabolism (here suggesting maple syrup urine disease) are enzyme defects causing toxic accumulation.

questions.q: A 9-month-old had 3 days of fever (40 C) and developed a maculopapular rash after the fever went away. Most likely cause?
questions.e: Rash after defervescence is the hallmark of roseola.

questions.q: A 5-year-old has high fever, cough, coryza and red eyes, with a rash that started on the face and spread downward over 3 days. Which best describes the measles rash?
o: Itchy vesicles that crust over time
Maculopapular, starts on the face, spreads to trunk and limbs, often confluent
Well-defined scaly plaque in a butterfly distribution
questions.e: Measles: 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots, then a cephalocaudal confluent maculopapular rash.

questions.q: A term newborn has microcephaly, micrognathia, microphthalmia, low-set ears, iris coloboma, postaxial polydactyly (7 fingers each hand), cleft palate, a VSD murmur, and rocker-bottom feet. Most likely cause?
questions.e: Patau: cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, coloboma/microphthalmia, holoprosencephaly. Rocker-bottom feet occur in both T13 and T18, but polydactyly and coloboma point to T13.

questions.q: In a patient with poorly controlled diabetes, HbA1c reflects glucose control over approximately:
questions.e: HbA1c reflects the average over the RBC lifespan, about 2-3 months.

questions.q: A 2-week-old preterm (800 g) on formula since day 2 has bloody stools, is pale and sick, with a distended tender abdomen and air in the bowel wall on X-ray. BP 40/20. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pneumatosis intestinalis in a formula-fed preterm = NEC. Stop feeds, NG decompression, IV antibiotics.

questions.q: A 4-week-old formula-fed infant has jaundice, poor feeding, vomiting, dark urine, pale stools and high direct bilirubin. Most important to investigate?
questions.e: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with pale stools needs urgent evaluation for biliary atresia.

questions.q: A neonate develops jaundice. Mother is O+, baby is A+, Coombs test positive. Cause?
questions.e: Group O mothers have IgG anti-A/anti-B that crosses the placenta. Both are Rh positive so Rh disease is excluded.

questions.q: Clear case of biliary atresia with pale stool and high direct bilirubin. Which is the gold standard among these for diagnosis?
questions.e: Among these options, liver biopsy. The definitive gold standard is intraoperative cholangiography. Ultrasound (triangular cord sign, absent gallbladder) is supportive only.

questions.q: Definition of prematurity:
questions.e: Preterm = birth before 37 completed weeks.

questions.q: An 18-month-old girl has blood-streaked stool, positive for occult blood. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Most common cause of blood-streaked stool in toddlers.

questions.q: A 9-month-old has fever 38.7, ear pulling, and a bulging erythematous tympanic membrane with purulent effusion. Most likely organism?
questions.e: AOM: S. pneumoniae, non-typeable H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis.

questions.q: A child has recurrent chest infections and oral thrush. No T cells, but B cells and NK cells are present. Diagnosis?
questions.e: T-B+NK+ SCID (e.g., IL-7R alpha defect). XLA has absent B cells with normal T cells.

questions.q: A 2-year-old is below the 3rd percentile for weight and height with frequent respiratory infections, irritability, visible muscle wasting and dry skin, but no edema. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe wasting without edema = marasmus. Edema is the hallmark of kwashiorkor.

questions.q: A 1-year-old has a normal palpable thyroid gland, elevated TSH and low T4. What do you suspect?
questions.e: Gland present and in place (or goitrous) with primary hypothyroidism points to dyshormonogenesis. Dysgenesis = absent/ectopic gland. Central gives low/normal TSH.

questions.q: Which physiological change occurs in the normal post-natal cardiopulmonary transition?
questions.e: Lung expansion and oxygen drop PVR, pulmonary flow rises; prostaglandins fall and the ductus closes.

questions.q: An 11-year-old has 1 day of right-sided abdominal pain, fever 37.9, vomiting, HR 112 and rebound tenderness in the RIF. Most likely cause?
questions.e: Classic acute appendicitis.

questions.q: An asthmatic child in an exacerbation has pH 7.49, low CO2, HCO3 21. Gas changes?
questions.e: Early asthma attack: hyperventilation lowers CO2. A "normal" or rising CO2 in an attack is an ominous sign of fatigue.

questions.q: A 9-year-old boy was recently diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome. Which is an indication for renal biopsy?
questions.e: Biopsy if features atypical for minimal change: age <1 or >12, persistent hypertension, gross hematuria, low C3, renal impairment, or steroid resistance.

questions.q: A 9-year-old collapses during soccer practice without warning. His father died suddenly at 40. Next step in evaluation?
o: ECG and echocardiogram to look for a cardiac cause
questions.e: Exertional syncope + family history of sudden death = cardiac until proven otherwise (HCM, long QT, etc.).

questions.q: A 26-month-old speaks single words only (20-word vocabulary), does not respond when his mother talks to him, is picky about foods and gets angry when his face is held. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Speech delay + poor social response + restricted interests + sensory aversion = ASD. A hearing test is still part of every speech-delay workup.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl is short (3rd percentile height, 35th weight), Tanner 2 breasts, no pubic hair, bone age 11 years. Her father was short as a teenager and is now 177 cm. Management?
questions.e: Delayed bone age + delayed but started puberty + family history of late growth = constitutional delay.

questions.q: A few-month-old infant has a mild fever (around 37.8) and looks alert and playful at the vaccine visit. What is correct?
o: Minor illness and low-grade fever are not contraindications to immunization
questions.e: Only moderate-severe acute illness warrants deferral.

questions.q: A child has fever, lethargy, neck stiffness and irritability. CSF is turbid with high WBC (mainly polymorphs), high protein and low glucose. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Neutrophils + high protein + low glucose = bacterial. TB: lymphocytes, very high protein, low glucose. Viral: lymphocytes, normal glucose.

questions.q: An 8-year-old has weight and height above the 95th percentile, BMI 30, looks older than peers, otherwise normal exam. Most appropriate management?
questions.e: First-line for pediatric obesity is intensive family-based lifestyle change. Tall stature suggests exogenous obesity (endocrine causes are usually short).

questions.q: A 5-year-old in PICU on insulin infusion and fluids for DKA: Na 138, K 2.8, Cl 101, HCO3 22. Most likely cause of the low potassium?
questions.e: Insulin drives K into cells. Total body K is depleted in DKA; add K to fluids once urine output confirmed and K <5.5.

questions.q: A 5-month-old with 3 days of severe diarrhea is lethargic and dehydrated. pH 7.22, HCO3 15, PaCO2 32. Primary disturbance?
questions.e: Low pH, low HCO3, low PaCO2. Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x 15 + 8 = 30.5 (+/-2), so compensation is appropriate.

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl with speech delay has a flat facial profile, upslanting eyes and a single palmar crease. Which blood test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.e: Karyotype confirms trisomy 21 and identifies translocations (important for recurrence risk). FISH is rapid but does not show translocation.

questions.q: A 3-month-old girl born breech is suspected to have developmental dysplasia of the hip. Best diagnostic modality?
questions.e: Ultrasound before ~4-6 months (femoral head not ossified). X-ray after that.

questions.q: An exclusively breastfed 5-day-old term boy had all standard newborn care and is normal on exam. Without supplementation, he is at greatest risk of:
questions.e: Breast milk is low in vitamin D; give 400 IU/day. Vitamin K was given at birth, and iron stores last about 4-6 months.

questions.q: An 18-hour-old term formula-fed baby is jaundiced. Mother O+, baby A+, retics 10%, total bilirubin 13, direct 1, direct Coombs positive. Underlying pathophysiology?
o: Immune-mediated hemolysis from blood group incompatibility
questions.e: Jaundice in the first 24 h + Coombs positive + reticulocytosis = ABO hemolytic disease.

questions.q: A 5-year-old with nephrotic syndrome develops renal vein thrombosis. Which blood abnormality contributes to this complication?
questions.e: Urinary loss of antithrombin III + increased hepatic clotting factors + hemoconcentration = hypercoagulable state.

questions.q: All of the following are part of high-quality CPR EXCEPT:
o: Allow the chest to fully recoil
Chest depressed at least 2/3 of its AP diameter
questions.e: Depth is at least 1/3 of the AP diameter, not 2/3.

questions.q: A fully vaccinated girl develops muscle weakness, loss of deep tendon reflexes and hypotonia. Her classmates have hand-foot-mouth disease. Most likely cause?
questions.e: Enterovirus A71 (a cause of HFMD) can cause acute flaccid myelitis. Vaccinated, so polio unlikely.

questions.q: A 6-week-old has persistent non-bilious vomiting, dehydration and visible peristalsis. Most likely electrolyte disturbance?
questions.e: Pyloric stenosis: loss of gastric HCl gives hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (paradoxical aciduria late).

questions.q: A 23-month-old hospitalized for severe malnutrition received inappropriately rapid NG feeding. Which lab value is most concerning as an iatrogenic complication?
questions.e: Refeeding syndrome: insulin surge shifts phosphate (and K, Mg) into cells. Start feeds slowly and monitor.

questions.q: A 2-year-old wakes at night with inspiratory noisy breathing, marked retractions, nasal flaring and a barking cough after 2 days of mild URTI. What will be done in the emergency department?
o: Observation for hypoxia and dehydration alone
Inhaled epinephrine and a dose of steroids
questions.e: Moderate-severe croup: nebulized epinephrine + dexamethasone. Observe 2-4 h after epinephrine for rebound.

questions.q: A 5-year-old girl is inattentive at home and school, refuses to talk to parents or peers, prefers playing alone. Normal physical and neurological exam. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Social communication deficits and preference for solitary play point to ASD.

questions.q: A 12-year-old ate peanuts and 10 minutes later has lip angioedema, urticaria, stridor and hypotension. Underlying pathophysiology?
o: IgE-mediated degranulation of mast cells and basophils releasing histamine and other mediators
questions.e: Anaphylaxis is a type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.q: An 18-hour-old term formula-fed neonate is jaundiced. Mother O+, baby A+. Most important investigation to order?
questions.e: Early jaundice with possible ABO setup: direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, plus bilirubin, blood group, retics.

questions.q: A post-term (42 weeks) baby born through thick meconium needed PPV and intubation. Cord pH 6.8, HCO3 8, Apgar 3 and 4, hypotonic with possible seizures. Which treatment improves long-term neurological outcome?
questions.e: Moderate-severe HIE: cooling within 6 hours of birth.

questions.q: At 5 minutes, a 28-week newborn in a plastic wrap is on CPAP 5 cmH2O with FiO2 70%, pink, well perfused, HR 135. Main reason for his respiratory distress?
questions.e: RDS (hyaline membrane disease) is inversely related to gestational age.

questions.q: A 10-year-old who drinks fresh camel milk on his grandfather's farm has 2 weeks of recurrent fever spikes, drenching night sweats, arthralgia, tender lymph nodes, relative bradycardia and raised AST/ALT. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Undulant fever + sweats + arthralgia + raw camel milk = brucellosis.

questions.q: A term neonate delivered for cord prolapse has a secure airway. Despite PPV with corrective maneuvers, HR is 52. After 1 minute of compressions HR is 48. Best next step?
o: Epinephrine via ETT until vascular access is established
questions.e: HR <60 despite 30 s effective ventilation and 60 s of compressions with 100% O2: epinephrine (IV/UVC preferred; ETT while access is obtained).

questions.q: A 13-year-old has 7 days of fever, nausea, non-productive cough, headache, fatigue, myalgia and arthralgia, now dyspnea. Scattered wheezes, bilateral interstitial opacities on CXR. Most likely organism?
questions.e: Atypical pneumonia in school-age children: gradual onset, extrapulmonary symptoms, interstitial pattern. Treat with a macrolide.

questions.q: A 4-year-old has had fever for 5 days and you suspect Kawasaki disease. Which is a diagnostic criterion?
questions.e: Criteria: fever >=5 days + 4 of: non-exudative bilateral conjunctivitis, oral changes (cracked lips, strawberry tongue), polymorphous rash, extremity changes, unilateral cervical node >1.5 cm.

questions.q: A 20 kg 5-year-old ingested 500 mg of paracetamol 10 hours ago and is asymptomatic. Next step?
questions.e: 500 mg / 20 kg = 25 mg/kg, well below the ~150-200 mg/kg toxic threshold for acute ingestion.

questions.q: Which vaccine can be given to a child with SCID?
questions.e: Live vaccines (BCG, MMR, rotavirus, varicella, OPV) are contraindicated in SCID. Inactivated vaccines are safe (though response may be poor).

questions.q: A 3-week-old has high fever, irritability, lethargy, poor feeding and leukocytosis (sepsis features). Best empirical antibiotics?
questions.e: Official key: ampicillin + cefuroxime. Note: most guidelines use ampicillin + a third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime) for late-onset neonatal sepsis, since cefuroxime has poor CSF penetration. Know the key's answer for this exam.

questions.q: A 5-year-old wakes screaming at night, frightened, unaware of surroundings, hard to console, for several minutes, and does not remember in the morning. He also has vivid dreams he can describe. Diagnosis for the screaming episodes?
questions.e: Night terrors: NREM, first third of night, inconsolable, no recall. The recalled dreams are nightmares.

questions.q: A 10-year-old has 2 years of cough and dyspnea worse at night and with exercise, triggered by dust. Which test most assists diagnosis of asthma?
questions.e: Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility (FEV1 increase >=12%) in children >5-6 years.

questions.q: An 18-month-old due for vaccines including varicella was exposed to active varicella at kindergarten this morning. What should the mother be told?
o: Skip this set and resume at 24 months
Come in to check serologic immunity first
No need to vaccinate; natural exposure gives immunity
Come to the clinic anyway; keep immunizations on schedule
questions.e: Varicella vaccine within 3-5 days of exposure can prevent or modify disease. Exposure is not a contraindication.

questions.q: A healthy 22 kg child is to receive maintenance IV fluids before surgery. Maintenance rate?

A 5-year-old unvaccinated girl has severe sore throat, drooling, high fever and increasing breathing difficulty. Looks toxic, sits on her mother's lap refusing to move, tachypneic. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hib epiglottitis: toxic, drooling, tripod, muffled voice. Keep calm; secure the airway in the OR.

questions.q: A neonate with 2 days of vomiting, poor sucking, afebrile: pH 7.28, CO2 29, HCO3 14. To calculate the anion gap you need:
questions.e: AG = Na - (Cl + HCO3).

questions.q: A 3-year-old sitting upright, drooling and distressed with stridor and retractions. What is important when assessing suspected upper airway obstruction?
o: Keep the child in a crowded area
questions.e: Agitation can precipitate complete obstruction. Let the child stay with the parent in a position of comfort; no throat exam or IV until the airway is secured.

questions.q: A 5-year-old has 6 days of fever, conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, hand swelling, diffuse rash and cervical lymphadenopathy. Which medication in initial treatment lessens the risk of complications?
questions.e: IVIG 2 g/kg (plus aspirin) reduces coronary aneurysm risk from ~25% to <5%.

questions.q: A friend advises giving fresh cow's milk instead of formula to a 2-month-old. Before 1 year, cow's milk puts the baby at risk of:
questions.e: Cow's milk is low in iron, inhibits absorption, and causes occult GI blood loss.

questions.q: A 3-week-old has frequent milky vomiting, abdominal distension and a small, fixed RUQ mass. Advice for first initial management?
questions.e: Pyloric stenosis is not a surgical emergency. Correct dehydration and alkalosis first, then pyloromyotomy.

questions.q: A 10 kg 1-year-old has fever, vomiting, acute diarrhea, HR 150, RR 50 with deep breaths, decreased turgor, lethargy, CRT 3 s. Next step?
o: Half normal saline bolus 200 mL over 30 min
Normal saline bolus 200 mL over 30 min
D5 half normal saline at 40 mL/hour
questions.e: Severe dehydration with poor perfusion: 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus. Hypotonic fluids are never used for boluses.

questions.q: A 2-week-old born at 36 weeks weighed 2.4 kg at birth and weighs 2.4 kg now. Parents are worried about intake. What would you advise?
questions.e: Regaining birth weight by 2 weeks is expected. Source PDF notes "Dr. Ahmed says this is the right answer."

questions.q: A child received IVIG for Kawasaki disease and is now due for his 2-year (live) vaccines. Expected effect on the vaccine?
questions.e: Official key: unchanged (one copy of this question in the PDF marks it "not sure"). Note: standard guidance (CDC/AAP) is that IVIG antibodies blunt the response to live vaccines like MMR and varicella, so they are delayed about 11 months after high-dose IVIG.

questions.q: A 12-hour-old infant born by C-section is jittery and hypoglycemic; the mother has diabetes. Likely cause of hypoglycemia?
questions.e: Fetal hyperinsulinism from maternal hyperglycemia persists after birth.

questions.q: A child has red urine following an upper respiratory infection. Urinalysis: 2+ protein, 20-30 RBC/HPF, dysmorphic RBCs. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Synpharyngitic hematuria (1-2 days after URTI) = IgA nephropathy. PSGN occurs 1-3 weeks after infection with low C3.

questions.q: A school-age child has streptococcal pharyngitis confirmed by rapid test. Antibiotics are started to prevent which serious complication?
questions.e: Treatment within 9 days prevents rheumatic fever. It does NOT prevent PSGN.

questions.q: A child with beta thalassemia major on chronic transfusions. Which complication will be seen?
questions.e: Transfusional hemosiderosis (heart, liver, endocrine). Needs chelation. The other options are sickle cell complications.

questions.q: A child has progressive cognitive decline. Parents say he had a viral exanthem 10 years ago. Most likely pathogen?
questions.e: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), 7-10 years after measles.

questions.q: A 14-year-old Saudi girl has jaundice after a week of flu-like illness. She recently swam in pools and beaches in Bahrain and donated blood a month ago. ALT 1225, AST 340, bilirubin 6.6, HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, anti-HCV negative, anti-HEV IgM negative. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fecal-oral exposure + acute hepatitis. Anti-HBs positive with negative HBsAg = immune (vaccinated). Confirm with anti-HAV IgM.

questions.q: What is the daily fluid requirement for an 18 kg child?
questions.e: Holliday-Segar: 100x10 + 50x8 = 1000 + 400 = 1400 mL/day.

questions.q: A child has intermittent asthma. What should be prescribed?
questions.e: Current GINA guidance: do not treat with SABA alone; use low-dose ICS whenever SABA is taken (6-11 y) or as-needed ICS-formoterol (12+ y). Another question in the PDF has the same answer ("inhaled corticosteroids when taking albuterol").

questions.q: A family follows a strict vegan diet. Which deficiency is expected?
questions.e: B12 is found almost only in animal foods. Iron can also be low, but B12 is the classic answer.

questions.q: An 8-year-old girl was dry at night until age 6, now wets frequently at night. No UTIs, no daytime symptoms, recent school stress. Most likely contributing factor?
questions.e: Secondary enuresis (after >=6 months dry) is often triggered by stress. Still screen urine for UTI and glucose.

questions.q: A 9-month-old has fever of 38.9 for 3 days, looks well, with no focus of infection. Next best step?
o: Empirical antibiotics and reassess in 48 h
questions.e: UTI is the most common serious bacterial infection in febrile infants without a source.

questions.q: A 3-year-old has 6 days of fever, conjunctivitis, lymph node enlargement and a maculopapular rash. What will you see on CBC?
questions.e: Kawasaki: leukocytosis, normocytic anemia, raised ESR/CRP, and thrombocytosis (peaks in the 2nd-3rd week).

questions.q: A neonate is born with a myelomeningocele. Best time for surgery?
questions.e: Early closure (within 48-72 h) reduces the risk of infection (ventriculitis/meningitis).

questions.q: A 4-month-old's head circumference is above the 98th percentile, with normal development and neurological exam. The father and his family have large heads. Next step?
o: Reassure and continue to monitor development
Urgent brain CT to rule out hydrocephalus
questions.e: Benign familial macrocephaly. Measure parents' heads; follow HC growth velocity.

questions.q: A 6-year-old has fever, malaise and a slapped-cheek rash followed by a lacy body rash. Which complication is most associated with this infection in sickle cell anemia?
questions.e: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors; transient red cell aplasia is dangerous with short RBC survival.

questions.q: A 15-year-old collapses suddenly while sitting in a class exam, with a few seconds of twitching, then several minutes of confusion. First episode. First investigation?
questions.e: Official key: EEG. Twitching followed by several minutes of post-ictal confusion points to a seizure. Note: many references still get an ECG in any first unexplained loss of consciousness to exclude arrhythmia.

questions.q: In which condition would you strongly advise against breastfeeding?
o: Mother has active untreated pulmonary tuberculosis
questions.e: Separate until the mother has had about 2 weeks of treatment (expressed milk can be given). Other contraindications: HIV (in high-resource settings), galactosemia, HTLV.

questions.q: A child begins to copy a square, hop on one foot and ask "why" and "how" questions. Most likely age?
questions.e: 4 y: copies square (some texts: cross at 4, square 4-5), hops, tells stories, "why" questions.

questions.q: A well, afebrile 4-year-old has small perioral vesicles that rupture leaving honey-colored crusts. Initial management?
questions.e: Localized impetigo: topical mupirocin or fusidic acid. Oral antibiotics for extensive disease.

questions.q: A 2-day-old has blue lips and tongue, SpO2 84% on room air, not improving with 100% oxygen. What best differentiates central from peripheral cyanosis?
o: Discoloration of mucous membranes and tongue
questions.e: Central cyanosis involves the tongue and mucous membranes. Failure to rise with O2 suggests cyanotic CHD.

questions.q: A 6-month-old has episodes of drawing up the legs, inconsolable crying and "red currant jelly" stool, is irritable with a distended abdomen and a palpable right-sided mass. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Ileocolic intussusception (peak 6-36 months). Ultrasound (target sign), then air/contrast enema reduction.

questions.q: A healthy 7-year-old has brief staring spells with eyelid fluttering, provoked by hyperventilation; EEG shows 3-Hz spike-and-wave. Most appropriate drug?
questions.e: First-line for childhood absence epilepsy. Carbamazepine can worsen absences.

questions.q: A 4-year-old has fever and an itchy rash that started on the trunk and spread to the face, scalp and arms, with lesions in different stages (macules, papules, "dewdrop on a rose petal" vesicles, crusts), sparing palms and soles. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Centripetal rash with crops at different stages = varicella.

questions.q: A 20 kg 6-year-old has severe dehydration. Initial isotonic saline bolus volume?
questions.e: 20 mL/kg x 20 kg = 400 mL.

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy, toilet trained 4 months ago, has abdominal pain, frequency, new bedwetting and odd-smelling urine. Last bowel movement 3 days ago. Dipstick: leukocyte esterase, nitrite, blood positive; gram-negative rods. Strongest risk factor?
questions.e: Bladder and bowel dysfunction (constipation) is a major risk factor for UTI in toilet-trained children. No features here suggest PUV.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea is 140 cm tall with no breast tissue and Tanner 3 pubic hair. Mother 173 cm, father 178 cm. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Short stature despite tall parents + absent breast development (ovarian failure) = Turner (45,X). Pubic hair from adrenal androgens is preserved.

questions.q: A 14-year-old has asymptomatic isolated proteinuria on routine urinalysis, confirmed on repeat, with normal BP and renal function. Best next step?
questions.e: First-morning sample distinguishes orthostatic (benign) proteinuria from persistent proteinuria.

questions.q: A 3-year-old has high fever, lethargy, CRT 4 s, weak pulse, BP 85/50, mottled and minimally responsive. Initial management?
questions.e: Septic shock: fluid boluses and antibiotics within the first hour. LP is deferred in an unstable child.

questions.q: A 2-year-old has a painless limp for months, limited left hip abduction, Trendelenburg gait and leg length discrepancy. X-ray: shallow acetabulum with superolateral displacement of the femoral head. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Late-presenting DDH. Perthes occurs at 4-8 y with femoral head avascular necrosis.

questions.q: Healthy first-cousin parents have a 3-year-old with cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive). Recurrence risk in each future pregnancy?
questions.e: Both parents are obligate carriers: 1 in 4 affected each pregnancy.

questions.q: A 3-year-old in DKA (glucose 700, pH 7.0, HCO3 8, 10% dehydrated). Most appropriate action to decrease the risk of cerebral edema?
o: Replace ongoing urinary losses with 0.2% saline
questions.e: Deficit replaced evenly over 24-48 h with isotonic fluids. Bicarbonate and hypotonic fluids increase cerebral edema risk.

questions.q: A newborn at 38 weeks delivered by emergency C-section for cord prolapse has arterial pH 6.89 at 30 minutes, SpO2 97%, lethargy, generalized hypotonia and weak suck. Management will include:
questions.e: Moderate-severe encephalopathy after a sentinel event with severe acidosis = HIE; cool within 6 h.

questions.q: A 4-week-old has persistent jaundice since birth, pale stools, dark urine, hepatomegaly. Bilirubin 7.2 (direct 5.6), GGT very high, HIDA shows no excretion after 24 h. Next best step?
questions.e: Biliary atresia: intraoperative cholangiogram confirms, then Kasai as early as possible (best before 60 days). Transplant if Kasai fails.

questions.q: A healthy term 2-month-old in Saudi Arabia comes for routine vaccines. According to the local schedule, which vaccines are given now?
o: DTaP, IPV, Hib, Hepatitis B, PCV and Rotavirus
questions.e: Saudi schedule at 2, 4, 6 months: hexavalent (DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB), PCV, rotavirus.

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl suddenly starts wheezing right after opening holiday gifts; her brother received toy cars with detachable wheels. Most appropriate test?
questions.e: Foreign body aspiration: expiratory film shows air trapping on the affected side (decubitus films in young children who cannot cooperate). Rigid bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic. Source PDF: "answer by Dr. Dana".

questions.q: A 5-year-old girl has 8 weeks of intermittent right knee swelling and positive ANA. Other than uveitis, which systemic complication may develop in oligoarticular JIA?
questions.e: Oligoarticular JIA can cause local growth disturbance (leg length discrepancy). MAS/HLH is associated with systemic JIA.

questions.q: An 18-month-old girl has a "full" abdomen with an abdominal mass, hematuria and a solid renal mass on ultrasound. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Wilms: smooth flank mass not crossing midline, hematuria, hypertension, age 2-5. Neuroblastoma is adrenal, crosses midline, child looks ill.

questions.q: Which advice on introducing complementary foods is correct?
o: Avoid allergenic foods until after 1 year
Introduce one new food every 3-5 days
questions.e: One new food at a time helps identify reactions. Honey is avoided under 1 year (botulism). Juice is not recommended in infancy. No need to delay allergens.

questions.q: A child develops hemolytic uremic syndrome after bacterial gastroenteritis. Which lab finding suggests this diagnosis?
questions.e: HUS triad: microangiopathic (Coombs-negative) hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, AKI. LDH and retics are high.

questions.q: A 10-year-old has fever, polyarthritis, tachycardia and a systolic murmur. You suspect acute rheumatic fever. Next step to support the diagnosis?
questions.e: Jones criteria require evidence of preceding GAS infection (ASO, anti-DNase B, or positive culture). Echo assesses carditis.

questions.q: A 10-year-old on a rural livestock farm who drinks unpasteurized goat milk has 4 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue, weight loss, musculoskeletal pain and mild hepatosplenomegaly. Blood cultures pending. Next lab test?
questions.e: Brucella serology: SAT titer >=1:160 (or >=1:320 in endemic areas) supports diagnosis.

questions.q: A 10-year-old has 3 days of watery diarrhea, is thirsty, active, with mildly dry mucous membranes, CRT 2 s, taking sips without vomiting. Next step?
questions.e: Mild-moderate dehydration: ORS (50-100 mL/kg over 4 h). Antidiarrheals are not used in children.

questions.q: A Saudi mother with HIV on ART has a high viral load. What feeding advice is appropriate for her infant?
o: Commercially prepared formula instead of breastfeeding
Treat infant with antiretrovirals and then breastfeed
questions.e: Where safe formula is available, HIV-positive mothers (especially with detectable viral load) should not breastfeed.

questions.q: Which factor indicates pre-renal acute kidney injury in children?
questions.e: Pre-renal: kidneys avidly retain Na and concentrate urine (FeNa <1%, urine osm >500). FeNa >2% suggests ATN.

questions.q: A 1-year-old has fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and a descending maculopapular rash. Hallmark diagnostic feature in the prodromal stage?
o: Redness and swelling of the Stensen duct opening
questions.e: Koplik spots (white spots on buccal mucosa) appear 1-2 days before the rash. Stensen duct redness is mumps.

questions.q: A midwife wants to give an intramuscular injection for routine neonatal care. What is it?
questions.e: 1 mg IM vitamin K at birth prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding. (Hepatitis B, not A, is the birth vaccine.)

questions.q: A 10-year-old girl has chronic rhinorrhea, nasal itch, sneezing, dark circles under her eyes and pale boggy mucosa. Which is true?
o: Skin testing is performed to identify causative allergens
Intranasal decongestants are the main treatment
It is a type III hypersensitivity disorder
Eosinophils release mediators in the early phase
questions.e: Allergic rhinitis is type I. Mast cells drive the early phase; eosinophils the late phase. Intranasal steroids are first-line; topical decongestants cause rebound.

questions.q: A 10-year-old was just discharged after an asthma exacerbation. Advice to prevent future exacerbations?
o: Start oral antibiotics at the onset of any URTI
Provide a written asthma action plan
questions.e: Written action plans, controller adherence, inhaler technique and trigger avoidance reduce exacerbations.

questions.q: A 4-year-old has fever, tachypnea and retractions; CXR confirms lobar pneumonia. Most likely etiology?
questions.e: Pneumococcus is the leading cause of lobar pneumonia. Mycoplasma is more common in school-age children with interstitial patterns.

questions.q: A 12 kg 2-year-old with viral gastroenteritis has HR 130, otherwise normal vitals, looks tired, cries with slight tears, moist mucosa. Most appropriate rehydration?
o: D10 normal saline 120 mL over 30 minutes
Commercial low-carb, no-sodium drink 750 mL over 4 hours
Oral solution with 1:1 glucose/sodium content, 600 mL over 6 hours
questions.e: Mild dehydration: ORS (glucose and sodium in a balanced ratio for co-transport), about 50 mL/kg (600 mL). Free water and sodium-free drinks risk hyponatremia.

questions.q: Which test is used to diagnose HIV in infants less than 18 months old?
questions.e: Maternal antibodies make antibody tests (ELISA, Western blot) unreliable before 18 months.

questions.q: Parents are concerned about MMR. Which is a valid contraindication?
questions.e: Anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component is a contraindication. MMR does not cause autism.

questions.q: In children with chronic kidney disease, which is the most effective strategy to slow progression?
o: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitors
questions.e: BP control and reducing proteinuria with ACEi/ARB slow CKD progression (ESCAPE trial).

questions.q: A 10-year-old has fever, polyarthritis, tachycardia, tachypnea and a systolic murmur. You suspect acute rheumatic fever. Which is a major criterion?
questions.e: Major (J♥NES): Joints (polyarthritis), carditis, nodules (subcutaneous), erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea. Fever is minor.

questions.q: An unvaccinated 4-year-old has fever and a pruritic vesicular rash in different stages. Her immunocompromised sister had a painful unilateral truncal vesicular rash. Which is true?
o: Immunocompromised patients usually have mild breakthrough illness
The causative organism is an RNA virus
It can be complicated by necrotizing fasciitis from GAS
questions.e: VZV (a DNA virus) spreads by respiratory droplets and vesicle fluid. Secondary GAS infection including necrotizing fasciitis is a key complication. It is severe in the immunocompromised.

questions.q: Which vaccine should NOT be given to a child with SCID?
questions.e: Measles vaccine is live attenuated.

questions.q: A 2-year-old with femoral osteomyelitis on IV antibiotics is afebrile with improving inflammatory markers after 72 hours. Next step?
o: Switch to oral antibiotics for a total of 3-4 weeks
questions.e: Early IV-to-oral switch once clinically improved and CRP falling. Total course usually 3-4 weeks.

questions.q: A 20 kg 5-year-old ingested paracetamol. If the serum level is above the treatment line on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, next step?
questions.e: Level above the treatment line (4-hour level or later) = give NAC.

questions.q: A 6-year-old has persistent proteinuria on dipstick at a routine check, otherwise normal exam and no family history. Most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Quantify first with a (first-morning) UPCR: normal <0.2 mg/mg, nephrotic >2.

questions.q: A well-hydrated 30 kg 6-year-old is admitted for elective surgery. Maintenance IV volume for the next 24 hours?

A 2-month-old girl is fussy, sleepy, poorly feeding and difficult to console, afebrile, with a full fontanelle and dilated pupils. CBC, electrolytes and urinalysis are normal. CT shows subdural hematoma. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Subdural hematoma in a non-mobile infant without a clear history = abusive head trauma until proven otherwise. Do skeletal survey and fundoscopy for retinal hemorrhages.

questions.q: A previously healthy 7-year-old has 3 days of fever and headache and 1 day of abnormal movements, now lethargic with decreased consciousness. CSF is clear with mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, slightly high protein. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Altered consciousness + seizures + viral CSF picture = encephalitis (HSV until proven otherwise: start IV acyclovir).

questions.q: A 1-year-old has 2 days of irritability, poor feeding, strong-smelling pink urine, no urine since morning, fever 38.8, and cries when the lower abdomen is palpated. Next step?
questions.e: Obtain a reliable urine sample by catheterization before starting antibiotics (and it relieves possible retention). Source PDF marks this as "confirmed by dr".

questions.q: A mother asks how she will know her 9-year-old daughter is beginning puberty. First visible sign?
questions.e: Thelarche is the first sign of female puberty (age 8-13). Menarche comes about 2-2.5 years later.

questions.q: A 3-month-old has progressively worsening jaundice since birth, pale stools, dark urine, hepatomegaly and poor weight gain. Most definitive test to confirm biliary atresia?
o: CT of the liver and biliary tract
questions.e: Intraoperative cholangiogram is the gold standard.

questions.q: A 3-year-old with recurrent wheezing (admitted at 9 months for bronchiolitis). According to the modified Asthma Predictive Index, which increases the risk of asthma later in life?
questions.e: mAPI: >=4 wheezing episodes plus 1 major (parental asthma, atopic dermatitis, aeroallergen sensitization) or 2 minor (food sensitization, eosinophils >=4%, wheezing apart from colds). Sibling asthma is not a criterion.

questions.q: A school-age boy always interrupts class, doesn't like to sit down and doesn't follow rules. Diagnosis and treatment?
o: Autism spectrum disorder; speech and language therapy
questions.e: Hyperactivity/impulsivity across settings = ADHD. Treatment combines behavioral therapy and stimulants (methylphenidate) for school-age children.

questions.q: A 15-month-old unvaccinated boy has fever then a cephalocaudal maculopapular rash, with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis. Which is also seen in this disease?
o: Orchitis as a well-known post-pubertal complication
questions.e: Measles. Orchitis is mumps.

questions.q: A 3-year-old has 2 days of fever and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Which is a red flag in lymphadenitis?
questions.e: Red flags for malignancy: >4-6 weeks, >2-3 cm, hard/fixed/non-tender, supraclavicular, weight loss, night sweats, hepatosplenomegaly.

questions.q: A 13-year-old girl has abdominal pain and diarrhea after eating at a burger restaurant a week ago. Low Hb, high retics, high LDH, high urea and creatinine, schistocytes. Most likely organism?
questions.e: Undercooked beef is a classic source of E. coli O157:H7, the main cause of HUS.

questions.q: A 12-year-old girl with ESRD has bruising and nosebleeds, normal platelet count and prolonged bleeding time. Most likely cause?
questions.e: Uremic toxins impair platelet adhesion/aggregation. Treat with dialysis, desmopressin, correcting anemia.

questions.q: A patient has IgA deficiency. Which vaccine can be given?
questions.e: Inactivated vaccines are safe. Live vaccines (especially OPV) are generally avoided in immunodeficiency; pneumococcal is the safe choice here.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl who eats no animal products has pale conjunctiva and a high MCV. Which is expected to be deficient?
questions.e: Macrocytic anemia + vegan diet = B12 deficiency.

questions.q: A 4-month-old has DiGeorge syndrome. What is the cause of its immunodeficiency?
o: Absent or hypoplastic thymus with impaired T-cell function
questions.e: 22q11.2 deletion: third/fourth pharyngeal pouch defect: thymic hypoplasia (T-cell deficiency), hypocalcemia (parathyroid), conotruncal heart defects.

questions.q: A child has had two febrile seizures, no developmental delay, normal neurological exam and normal EEG. Likelihood of developing epilepsy?
o: Low, because the seizures are associated with fever
Potentially increased due to his history
questions.e: Risk after simple febrile seizures is about 1-2%, only slightly above the general population. Recurrent febrile seizures alone do not make it high.

questions.q: A child has brief spells of staring into space, unaware, with generalized spike-and-wave on EEG. Diagnosis and treatment?
questions.e: Ethosuximide first-line; valproate and lamotrigine are alternatives.

questions.q: A 3-week-old girl has large-volume vomiting after breastfeeds and an epigastric mass. What is the gold standard for diagnosis?
questions.e: US: pyloric muscle thickness >=3-4 mm, length >=15-17 mm.

questions.q: A well-appearing 5-year-old has 2 days of fever 38.5, mild ear pain and ear discharge. Bulging dull tympanic membrane with otorrhea. Next best step?
o: Symptomatic therapy and reassess in 48-72 h
Blood culture from ear and other tests
questions.e: Official key: symptomatic therapy and reassess in 48-72 h (watchful waiting in a well child over 2 years). Note: AAP guidance lists otorrhea as a reason to start antibiotics, so this answer differs from the AAP guideline.

questions.q: A child has petechiae and ecchymoses (no other bleeding), no family history, and platelet count 33,000. Best therapy?
questions.e: Newly diagnosed ITP with only skin bleeding: observation (ASH 2019), regardless of platelet count. Steroids or IVIG for mucosal/significant bleeding. Check what your lecture taught, as some teach treatment below a count threshold.

questions.q: A 7-year-old has pallor, fatigue and hepatosplenomegaly. Low Hb and low platelets. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bone marrow failure (anemia, thrombocytopenia) + organomegaly = ALL, the most common childhood cancer.

questions.q: A child has slurred speech and left facial twitching at night with no focal deficit. What will you see on EEG?
questions.e: Benign epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (Rolandic): nocturnal hemifacial seizures with drooling/speech arrest, good prognosis.

questions.q: You are following a 13-year-old with asthma. Which is a reliever therapy?
questions.e: Formoterol has a rapid onset, so budesonide-formoterol can be used as reliever (MART / as-needed ICS-formoterol). Salmeterol is slow-onset and is not a reliever.

questions.q: A child has wheezing and sudden cough that started when he was alone in a room. CXR shows unilateral hyperinflation. Asthma therapy gives no improvement. Next step?
questions.e: Unwitnessed choking + unilateral hyperinflation (ball-valve) = foreign body. Rigid bronchoscopy.

questions.q: A 9-month-old term girl has iron deficiency anemia. She had formula until 6 months, then baby foods and whole cow's milk. Which is correct?
o: Her age is atypical for iron deficiency
Full-term babies are at high risk of iron deficiency
Early introduction of cow's milk is the likely cause
Early introduction of solids is the likely cause
questions.e: Cow's milk before 12 months: low iron, poor bioavailability, occult GI blood loss.

questions.q: Which is an indication for renal biopsy in nephrotic syndrome?
questions.e: Gross hematuria, hypertension, low C3, renal failure, age <1 or >12, or steroid resistance suggest a lesion other than minimal change disease.

questions.q: A neonate is in shock (tachycardia, tachypnea, CRT >4 s). Cultures grow gram-positive cocci. Most likely organism?
questions.e: GBS is the leading cause of neonatal sepsis (with E. coli).

questions.q: A 2-week-old formula-fed neonate was 3.6 kg at birth and is now 2.8 kg. He sleeps about 18 hours. Main concern?
questions.e: 22% below birth weight at 2 weeks is abnormal (should have regained birth weight). 16-18 h sleep is normal for a newborn.

questions.q: A 5-year-old with GERD has failed conservative management. Next step?
questions.e: Step up to acid suppression (PPI/H2 blocker) after lifestyle measures fail. Fundoplication is reserved for refractory or life-threatening cases.

questions.q: All of the following are true about salicylate poisoning EXCEPT:
o: It causes respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis
questions.e: Salicylates cause respiratory ALKALOSIS (direct respiratory center stimulation) and high anion gap metabolic ACIDOSIS.

questions.q: A child has fever, headache and behavioral change. CSF is clear with normal glucose, slightly raised protein and lymphocytosis. Imaging shows temporal lobe involvement. Best next step?
questions.e: Temporal lobe encephalitis = HSV. Start IV acyclovir immediately; confirm with CSF HSV PCR.

questions.q: A 4-year-old has only received his 2- and 4-month vaccines. Appropriate action?
o: Give vaccines for his current age and catch up the missed ones
Give only current-age vaccines and ignore the missed ones
questions.e: Never restart a series. Continue where it stopped, following the catch-up schedule.

questions.q: A child with renal failure missed dialysis and looks sick. What will his blood gas show?
questions.e: Retained acids (sulfate, phosphate, urate) cause high AG metabolic acidosis in uremia.

questions.q: A child's BP is 114/74, between the 50th and 90th percentile. Next step?
o: Reassure the parents that it is normal
questions.e: <90th percentile is normal BP.

questions.q: A 4-month-old seen for an ear infection has a heart murmur. Which feature most suggests it needs further investigation?
questions.e: Pathological features: thrill (grade >=4), diastolic, pansystolic, loud, harsh, symptoms, abnormal S2. Innocent murmurs change with posture. 6 kg is normal at 4 months.

questions.q: A child can draw a cross/square. What is his age?
questions.e: Circle 3 y, cross 3-4 y, square 4 y, triangle 5 y.

questions.q: A 10-year-old has fever, exudative tonsillitis, prominent lymphadenopathy and lethargy. Amoxicillin was given; the next day she developed a maculopapular rash. She has splenomegaly. Cause of the rash?
questions.e: Infectious mononucleosis: amoxicillin/ampicillin causes a rash in most patients. Avoid contact sports due to splenomegaly.

questions.q: A mother does not want her infant to get varicella and MMR on the same day and asks to return in 2 weeks for the second. Best response?
o: If live vaccines are not given simultaneously, they must be separated by at least 28 days
Live vaccines may be given within 4 days of one another
Live vaccines may be given within 2 weeks of one another
Giving more than one live vaccine on the same day increases adverse reactions
questions.e: Interference: a second injectable live vaccine given within 28 days of the first may be less effective.

questions.q: An 8-year-old has not grown in height for 2 years. Which best approximates the normal prepubertal annual height gain?
questions.e: Prepubertal children grow about 5-6 cm/year. Less than 4 cm/year after age 3 needs evaluation.

questions.q: A child rides a tricycle, draws a cross and helps to dress himself. Expected age?
questions.e: 3 years: tricycle, copies circle/cross, helps dress, alternates feet on stairs.

questions.q: A patient with E. coli O157 has acute renal failure and anemia (HUS). What do you expect to see?
questions.e: Microangiopathic hemolysis: schistocytes, low haptoglobin, high LDH, thrombocytopenia.

questions.q: What is the earliest time you can give cow's milk?
questions.e: Whole cow's milk as a main drink from 12 months.

questions.q: A 3-week-old has microcephaly, periventricular calcifications and blindness. Most likely cause?
questions.e: CMV: periventricular calcification, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, sensorineural hearing loss. Toxoplasmosis gives diffuse calcifications + hydrocephalus.

questions.q: A 4-year-old has axillary freckling, 6 cafe-au-lait spots and neurological manifestations. Diagnosis?
questions.e: NF1 criteria: >=6 CALMs (>5 mm prepubertal), axillary/inguinal freckling, neurofibromas, optic glioma, Lisch nodules, bone lesions, first-degree relative.

questions.q: An 8-year-old has never been dry at night (3-4 wet nights/week), dry by day since 3, no urinary symptoms, normal exam and urinalysis; father wet until 9. Best next step?
o: Decrease fluids at bedtime and use a bedwetting alarm
questions.e: Primary monosymptomatic enuresis (strong family history). Behavioral measures and alarm first; desmopressin as alternative.

questions.q: DiGeorge syndrome is a defect in which arm of immunity?
questions.e: Thymic hypoplasia means a T-cell (cellular) immunodeficiency.

questions.q: A patient has G6PD deficiency with hemolysis. Which lab finding is true?
questions.e: Hemolysis: high retics, low haptoglobin, high LDH and indirect bilirubin; Heinz bodies and bite cells on smear.

questions.q: Oral rehydration solution (homemade) contains:
o: Half teaspoon salt and 6 teaspoons sugar in 1 liter of water
Half teaspoon salt and 6 teaspoons sugar in 1 liter of apple juice
Half teaspoon sugar and 6 teaspoons salt in 1 liter of water
Half teaspoon sugar and 6 teaspoons salt in 1 liter of apple juice
questions.e: WHO home recipe: 1/2 level teaspoon salt + 6 level teaspoons sugar in 1 L clean water.

questions.q: A 3-month-old ex-preterm was in the NICU for weeks and has just been discharged. Parents fear severe lower respiratory infection. What do you advise?
o: Just stick with the vaccination schedule
Palivizumab injection once a month during winter (RSV season)
Omalizumab injection once a month during winter
questions.e: Palivizumab (anti-RSV monoclonal) for high-risk infants (prematurity, CLD, significant CHD). Nirsevimab is a newer single-dose option. Omalizumab is anti-IgE.

questions.q: A 12-year-old girl has 2 weeks of fever and polyarthralgia; she looks well but pale. Urine shows traces of protein and blood. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Adolescent girl + fever + arthralgia + anemia + renal involvement = SLE.

questions.q: On urine dipstick, which of the following is heme-negative (red/pink urine without blood)?
questions.e: Urate crystals give pink/brick-colored diapers with a negative heme test. Glomerular causes contain RBCs (heme positive).

questions.q: A child has fever, sore throat and a unilateral, tender, erythematous cervical lymph node. Most likely causative agent?
questions.e: Acute unilateral pyogenic lymphadenitis: S. aureus and GAS. EBV and adenovirus give bilateral nodes; cat scratch is subacute and less tender. (The source notes list S. aureus.)

questions.q: A well 2-year-old has tender vesicular lesions on both feet, a few on his hands and tongue. Most likely cause?
questions.e: Hand, foot and mouth disease (Coxsackie A16, enterovirus A71).

questions.q: A 10-month-old weighing 8 kg is admitted. At what rate should maintenance IV fluids run?
questions.e: 4 mL/kg/h for the first 10 kg: 4 x 8 = 32 mL/h.

questions.q: A 5-month-old with bronchiolitis (bilateral wheeze) is not feeding well. Appropriate management?
questions.e: Bronchiolitis care is supportive: hydration (NG or IV), oxygen if SpO2 <90-92%, suction. Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not recommended routinely.

questions.q: In salicylate poisoning (early hyperglycemia, later hypoglycemia), which is an indication to give IV glucose?
questions.e: CNS glucose can be low even with normal serum glucose, so give dextrose for any altered mental status in salicylate toxicity.

questions.q: A 5-year-old is diagnosed with asthma. Appropriate way to take the inhaled treatment?
questions.e: Under ~6 years, pMDI + spacer (with mask if <4 y). DPIs need a strong inspiratory flow.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent otitis media and pneumonia; his maternal uncle has the same problem. Best initial test?
questions.e: Recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections in a boy with X-linked family history suggests XLA: start with serum IgG, IgA, IgM, then B-cell (CD19) count.

questions.q: A newborn has markedly enlarged head circumference with a bulging anterior fontanelle but is otherwise well. Next step?
o: Reassure, it is a genetic variant
questions.e: Bulging fontanelle + macrocephaly suggests raised ICP from hydrocephalus. Cranial US through the open fontanelle is the first test.

questions.q: A child has fever, sore throat, a sandpaper-like rash and strawberry tongue. Causative agent?
questions.e: Scarlet fever is caused by GAS erythrogenic toxin. Treat with penicillin/amoxicillin.

questions.q: A child receives varicella zoster immunoglobulin. What type of immunity is this?
questions.e: Pre-formed antibodies given medically = passive artificial. Maternal IgG across the placenta = passive natural.

questions.q: A preterm infant had perinatal brain damage involving the cortex and motor pathways (pyramidal tracts). Which diagnosis?
questions.e: Pyramidal/periventricular white matter injury (PVL in preterms) = spastic CP, often spastic diplegia. Basal ganglia injury = dyskinetic; cerebellar = ataxic.

questions.q: A child has facial angiofibromas and a history of seizures. Which is consistent with tuberous sclerosis?
questions.e: TSC skin signs: ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, ungual fibromas.

questions.q: An unvaccinated 4-month-old has fever, vomiting and non-bloody diarrhea without mucus. Likely cause?
questions.e: Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe dehydrating gastroenteritis in unvaccinated infants.

questions.q: A child has repeated seizures and cafe-au-lait spots on exam. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Cafe-au-lait macules are the hallmark of NF1. TSC has hypopigmented macules; Sturge-Weber has a port-wine stain.

questions.q: An exclusively breastfed 16-month-old has swelling at the wrists/arms. Expected labs?
